title: Sustained VM Read or Write Latency by Datastore
exclusions: Measures vSphere virtual-machine datastore read and write latency only from the two named metrics emitted by Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics. A row means the worse of the mean read or mean write latency was above the local 20-millisecond investigation threshold in two consecutive five-minute buckets for one VM/datastore pair. It does not identify device, kernel, queue, fabric, array, path, guest-filesystem, or application latency; prove user-visible impact; distinguish workload demand from a storage fault; calculate a percentile from averages; or authorize migration, path failover, storage rescan, or array changes. It does not cover host-only metrics, a VM with no metric points, a datastore dimension absent from collection, vSAN-specific health, capacity, inaccessible datastores, security attribution, or regulatory compliance. UC-2.1.4 has overlapping datastore-latency intent at a broader host/datastore grain; this record preserves the requested identity and is deliberately scoped to VM/datastore attribution.
evidence: After deployment, retain the version-controlled `UC-2.1.43 - Sustained VM Datastore Latency` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, search job IDs, triggered rows, exact Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics and Metrics Indexes versions, effective VM metric allow/deny settings, vCenter target and collection interval, metric/dimension inventory, source-freshness report, approved threshold and exception revisions, and dated positive and negative control outputs. For each finding preserve the two contributing five-minute buckets, VM UUID/MOID and display name, datastore, vCenter, hypervisor, read/write averages and peaks, point counts, same-window vSphere chart comparison, responder disposition, and any correlated storage or application evidence. These artifacts document collected telemetry and search behavior; this documentation-only review did not run the collector or SPL, approve 20 milliseconds for a production storage tier, or provide VMware, Splunk, storage-vendor, customer-SME, or runtime sign-off.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated metrics index, use an approved metric-ingest fixture to write `source=VMPerf:VirtualMachine`, `sourcetype=vmware_inframon:perf:datastore` points for `vcenter=vcsa-lab-01`, `uuid=421d-test-vm-43`, `moid=vm-43`, `name=latency-positive`, `datastore=ds-lab-01`, and `hypervisor=esx-lab-01`. In each of two adjacent completed five-minute buckets write `vmware.vm.datastore.totalReadLatency` values averaging 25 and 26 milliseconds respectively and `vmware.vm.datastore.totalWriteLatency` values averaging 8 and 9 milliseconds. Run the catalogue SPL with only the index changed and a time range containing those buckets. Expect exactly one row for the second bucket with `previous_worst_ms=25.00`, `worst_avg_ms=26.00`, `threshold_ms=20`, and nonzero current and previous point counts.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run four isolated cases. First, make both consecutive buckets' worse mean exactly 20.00 milliseconds; expect no row because the rule is strictly greater than 20. Second, make only one bucket 26 milliseconds and the adjacent bucket 19 milliseconds; expect no row because persistence is not met. Third, provide high host-scoped `vmware.esxihost.datastore.totalReadLatency` points but no VM-scoped metric; expect no row because the metric names are different. Fourth, omit or blank the VM identity or datastore dimension, or use a negative metric value; expect no finding because the qualified VM/datastore contract rejects the series. Preserve the generated points and search results; these are specified controls, not a claim that they have been executed.

dataSources: Metrics-index performance points collected from vCenter's PerformanceManager API by Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics (`Splunk_TA_vmware_inframon`, Splunkbase 5089) through its Data Collection Scheduler and Data Collection Nodes. The vendor-defined metrics index is `vmware-perf-metrics`; the queried metadata is `source=VMPerf:VirtualMachine` and `sourcetype=vmware_inframon:perf:datastore`. Required metric names are `vmware.vm.datastore.totalReadLatency` and `vmware.vm.datastore.totalWriteLatency`, both documented by Splunk as milliseconds and mapped from vSphere `datastore.average.totalReadLatency.millisecond` and `datastore.average.totalWriteLatency.millisecond`. Required dimensions are `_time`, `vcenter`, `uuid` or `moid`, `name`, `datastore`, and `hypervisor`; `host` is retained as collection metadata. Broadcom defines the underlying average counters as total latency, where total latency is kernel plus device latency, and exposes them by datastore instance for virtual machines and hosts. Confirm metric and dimension presence with `mcatalog` in the installed release before enabling the alert. Saved-search names and the 20-millisecond policy threshold are local choices; the metric names, source, source type, dimensions, units, and default index are add-on contracts.
app: Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics (`Splunk_TA_vmware_inframon`, Splunkbase 5089) version 5.0.0 or later; the Splunkbase default reviewed on 2026-07-29 is 5.0.1. Install a compatible Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics Indexes (`SA-VMWIndex-inframon`, Splunkbase 5602) version 4.2.1 or later on the indexer tier. Version 5.x supports vCenter/ESXi 7.0 and 8.0; verify the current Splunkbase platform matrix and Splunk dependency table before deployment. This API and metrics-index path is not supplied by Splunk Add-on for VMware ESXi Logs and is not a Universal Forwarder-only input.
spl:
| mstats avg(vmware.vm.datastore.totalReadLatency) AS avg_read_ms avg(vmware.vm.datastore.totalWriteLatency) AS avg_write_ms max(vmware.vm.datastore.totalReadLatency) AS peak_read_ms max(vmware.vm.datastore.totalWriteLatency) AS peak_write_ms count(vmware.vm.datastore.totalReadLatency) AS read_points count(vmware.vm.datastore.totalWriteLatency) AS write_points WHERE index="vmware-perf-metrics" source="VMPerf:VirtualMachine" sourcetype="vmware_inframon:perf:datastore" earliest=-25m@m latest=@m BY vcenter host uuid moid name datastore hypervisor span=5m
| eval entity_id=coalesce(uuid,moid), vm_name=coalesce(name,entity_id), datastore=trim(datastore)
| where len(entity_id)>0 AND len(datastore)>0 AND (read_points>0 OR write_points>0) AND (isnull(avg_read_ms) OR avg_read_ms>=0) AND (isnull(avg_write_ms) OR avg_write_ms>=0)
| eval worst_avg_ms=case(isnotnull(avg_read_ms) AND isnotnull(avg_write_ms),max(avg_read_ms,avg_write_ms),isnotnull(avg_read_ms),avg_read_ms,isnotnull(avg_write_ms),avg_write_ms), point_count=max(read_points,write_points), threshold_ms=20
| where worst_avg_ms>threshold_ms
| sort 0 vcenter entity_id datastore _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(_time) AS previous_bucket_time last(worst_avg_ms) AS previous_worst_ms last(point_count) AS previous_point_count BY vcenter entity_id datastore
| eval expected_bucket_start=floor((now()-120)/300)*300-300
| where _time-previous_bucket_time=300 AND _time=expected_bucket_start
| eval avg_read_ms=round(avg_read_ms,2), avg_write_ms=round(avg_write_ms,2), peak_read_ms=round(peak_read_ms,2), peak_write_ms=round(peak_write_ms,2), worst_avg_ms=round(worst_avg_ms,2), previous_worst_ms=round(previous_worst_ms,2)
| sort 0 - worst_avg_ms
| table _time vcenter hypervisor entity_id vm_name datastore read_points write_points point_count avg_read_ms avg_write_ms peak_read_ms peak_write_ms previous_point_count previous_worst_ms worst_avg_ms threshold_ms
description: Returns one row per virtual-machine/datastore pair when the worse of mean vSphere total read or total write latency exceeds 20 milliseconds in two adjacent five-minute buckets. The metrics-index search preserves VM, datastore, vCenter, hypervisor, current averages and peaks, point counts, and the prior bucket's value, while rejecting missing identity, missing datastore, and negative measurements.
value: Attributing persistent storage delay to a VM and its datastore gives virtualization, storage, and application owners a common investigation key. It helps them separate an isolated workload pattern from a shared datastore or host-path pattern, prioritize corroboration before service objectives are missed, and avoid treating a brief latency spike as sufficient evidence for a disruptive storage change.
implementation: Deploy Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics 5.0.0+ with a compatible Metrics Indexes package on the documented Scheduler, Data Collection Node, indexer, and search tiers. Configure vCenter API collection, retain the two VM datastore latency metrics and VM instance-level datastore dimensions, and verify their names, units, identity, and freshness with `mcatalog`/`mstats`. Save the search on a five-minute schedule with a two-minute data-delay allowance. Treat 20 milliseconds as a local investigation threshold that must be baselined by storage tier and workload; require two adjacent buckets, throttle on immutable VM ID plus datastore, and validate controls and vSphere parity before paging.
visualization: Build a current-findings table with bucket time, vCenter, hypervisor, VM name and immutable ID, datastore, read/write point counts, mean and peak read/write latency, prior worst mean, current worst mean, and threshold. Add a 24-hour line chart for the selected VM/datastore with separate `avg_read_ms` and `avg_write_ms` series and the approved policy line. Add a datastore heat map with VM rows, datastore columns, and `worst_avg_ms` color only after preserving the underlying grain, plus a source-health panel showing metric freshness, reporting VM/datastore pairs, missing dimensions, and negative values. Drill down by immutable entity ID and datastore into host peers, IOPS/throughput, tasks/events, and available array telemetry. Label every latency value `ms`; do not label it guest response time, DAVG, queue latency, percentile latency, or application latency.
dataModelAcceleration: No generic CIM or accelerated event-data variant is asserted. The source is an add-on-defined metrics index with two exact metric names and VMware identity dimensions, and `mstats` is the native optimized access path. A deployment may map derived results into a service model after proving parity, but must retain metric name, unit, VM identity, datastore, vCenter, bucket, point count, and read/write direction.

knownFalsePositives:
A row accurately reports the collected means under the qualified metric contract. A "false positive" here means the latency is expected, the local threshold is unsuitable, or identity/collection is wrong—not that an unrelated Linux process fabricated a vSphere counter.

1. **VADP backup, snapshot consolidation, clone, or Storage vMotion window** — Veeam or another VMware backup product, snapshot consolidation, cloning, and a planned relocation can drive real temporary I/O and latency. Match the VM ID, datastore, vCenter task/event, backup job ID, change owner, and bounded UTC window. Preserve the measurement as change evidence; suppress notification only for those exact entities and times.

2. **Approved database maintenance or batch processing** — SQL index rebuilds, data-warehouse loads, log compaction, and application batch jobs can create sustained legitimate storage demand. Compare application job telemetry, IOPS/throughput, completion status, and service objectives. Recurrence does not make harmful latency benign; suppress only when the workload owner has approved the measured envelope.

3. **Array replication, rebuild, tier movement, or controller maintenance** — A storage-platform rebuild, replication catch-up, cache warm-up, tier relocation, or controller failover may raise latency across many VM/datastore pairs. Correlate exact array volume, maintenance record, path state, and affected peer VMs. Route to the storage change owner; do not exempt the datastore after the approved window.

4. **Cold cache after VM power-on or migration** — A recently powered-on or migrated VM can briefly repopulate guest and storage caches. Verify the power/migration event and whether latency decays while service objectives remain healthy. This rule already requires two adjacent buckets; any additional suppression must be limited to the exact VM and bounded warm-up policy.

5. **Storage tier with a different approved latency objective** — NFS, VMFS on rotating media, all-flash, vVol, and remote or replicated storage can have materially different baselines. Compare the VM/datastore pair with its governed storage-tier objective and historical distribution. Replace the global threshold with a reviewed tier lookup only after proving keys and defaults; never silently call every tier healthy at 20 milliseconds.

6. **Duplicate collection or wrong datastore dimension** — Overlapping vCenter/DCN scope, duplicate metric forwarding, stale hierarchy, or collection without the intended instance-level datastore dimension can duplicate points or misattribute a VM. Compare metric point counts, `vcenter`, `uuid`/`moid`, `datastore`, `hypervisor`, scheduler scope, and vSphere inventory. Correct collection and identity rather than suppressing a data-quality defect.

**Safe suppression:** keep the catalogue SPL free of an invented lookup dependency. If local policy requires maintenance suppression, apply a governed lookup after condition formation, keyed by use-case ID, immutable `entity_id`, exact `datastore`, `valid_from_epoch`, `valid_until_epoch`, owner, ticket, and reason. Reject wildcard, expired, and open-ended entries; preserve unsuppressed results and source-health failures.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational vSphere storage-performance measurement; elevated latency alone does not establish adversary behavior)
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics 5.x source-type, metric, dimension, index, topology, and compatibility documentation; Splunk mstats syntax; and Broadcom datastore-counter semantics and latency-investigation guidance; field contract, SPL, controls, threshold governance, alerting, dashboard, and response specified but not executed on vCenter, a Data Collection Node, a metrics index, or live Splunk; no production, VMware, Splunk, storage-vendor, performance-SME, or customer sign-off

cost.search_load_notes: A five-minute scheduled `mstats` search reads two named metrics over 25 minutes from the purpose-built metrics index, groups by VM/datastore dimensions and five-minute buckets, then compares adjacent breaches. Metrics-index execution is optimized, but cardinality scales with reporting VM/datastore pairs and duplicate dimensions.
sources: vCenter PerformanceManager datastore read and write latency counters
Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics API collection

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and measurement boundary

Assign a VMware platform owner, a Splunk VMware-collection owner, a storage owner, and an application owner for every paged VM. Install Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics (Splunkbase 5089) 5.0.0 or later and a compatible Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics Indexes (Splunkbase 5602) 4.2.1 or later according to the current deployment matrix. The Splunkbase default observed during this review was 5.0.1, while the public requirements page documents the 5.x compatibility family; verify the exact supported Splunk, vCenter, ESXi, Python, and package combination before rollout. Version 5.x supports vCenter and ESXi 7.0/8.0 and requires Splunk Enterprise 9.3 or later for Scheduler/DCN components. Use the documented Data Collection Scheduler and Data Collection Nodes, API connectivity to vCenter, token-based DCS/DCN communication for 5.x, and the `vmware-perf-metrics` metrics index supplied by the Indexes package. Do not substitute the ESXi Logs add-on: syslog does not create these metric names.

The underlying vSphere counters are `datastore.totalReadLatency.average` and `datastore.totalWriteLatency.average`. Broadcom defines each as average milliseconds per read or write operation, with total latency equal to kernel plus device latency, and exposes datastore identity as an instance for virtual-machine and host providers. Splunk documents their VM metric names as `vmware.vm.datastore.totalReadLatency` and `vmware.vm.datastore.totalWriteLatency` under `source=VMPerf:VirtualMachine`, `sourcetype=vmware_inframon:perf:datastore`. This rule compares means of already averaged vSphere samples; it does not calculate request-weighted latency or a percentile. Preserve that limitation in dashboards and tickets.

## Step 1 — Configure and qualify metrics collection

On the Scheduler, register each DCN and vCenter using Splunk's Collection Configuration workflow and a vCenter account limited to the documented read/performance collection privileges. Install `SA-VMWIndex-inframon` on the indexer tier so `vmware-perf-metrics` exists as a metrics index. Keep the default VM datastore latency metrics in the VM metric allowlist; if a denylist is used, prove neither parameter value `datastore.average.totalReadLatency.millisecond` nor `datastore.average.totalWriteLatency.millisecond` is excluded. Enable VM instance-level collection so datastore is retained at the intended grain. Instance collection raises cardinality and ingest, so estimate reporting VM/datastore pairs before production enablement.

Use `mcatalog values(metric_name) WHERE index=vmware-perf-metrics` to prove both exact metric names exist. Then enumerate dimensions for each metric and inspect two known VMs with `mstats`. Confirm `source`, `sourcetype`, `vcenter`, `uuid`/`moid`, `name`, `datastore`, `hypervisor`, unit semantics, timestamps, and point cadence. Reconcile the datastore dimension with current vSphere inventory and test a multi-datastore VM; a single aggregate value is not equivalent to per-datastore attribution. Check duplicate series by vCenter, immutable VM ID, datastore, metric, and time. Build a separate freshness report for expected VM/datastore pairs. Silence is unknown coverage, never zero latency.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the search

Save the catalogue SPL as `UC-2.1.43 - Sustained VM Datastore Latency` and schedule it every five minutes. The 25-minute lookback covers several five-minute buckets. `mstats` reads only the two documented VM metrics and groups by the documented identity dimensions. It calculates current bucket means and peaks and counts available points. The first `where` rejects missing immutable identity, missing datastore, a bucket with neither metric, and negative means; one direction may legitimately be absent when no corresponding operation was observed. `worst_avg_ms` selects the larger available read/write mean without turning a missing direction into zero.

The rule first keeps buckets strictly above the local 20-millisecond threshold. `streamstats current=f window=1` attaches the prior breached bucket for the same vCenter, VM ID, and datastore. Requiring a 300-second difference prevents nonadjacent breaches from being called continuous. `expected_bucket_start` selects the newest completed five-minute bucket while allowing two minutes for collection/indexing; measure actual delay and increase that allowance only through change control. The output reports the second bucket of a two-bucket breach. Trigger when result count is greater than zero and throttle by `entity_id` plus `datastore`; do not throttle on mutable VM names.

Twenty milliseconds is an investigation policy, not a universal VMware failure boundary. Broadcom's device-latency guidance emphasizes magnitude, duration, storage technology, and scope, and distinguishes device latency from the total latency used here. Baseline each storage tier through representative business cycles, compare against application objectives and array guidance, and record the approved threshold. Do not call `avg()` a percentile and do not automate Storage vMotion, rescan, path failover, VM suspension, or array changes from this result.

## Step 3 — Validate semantics, persistence, and coverage

Run the positive control in an isolated metrics index. Create two adjacent completed buckets with read means of 25 and 26 milliseconds and write means of 8 and 9 for the same immutable VM/datastore dimensions. Confirm one result for the second bucket, the expected prior/current worst values, and nonzero point counts. Run exact-boundary tests at 20.00, one-bucket-only tests, host-metric substitution tests, negative values, missing identity, missing datastore, one-direction-only data, duplicate points, and a datastore change between buckets. Verify that different datastores for the same VM do not combine and that VM and host metric names cannot mix.

In a nonproduction or change-approved vCenter, choose at least one VM attached to multiple datastores. Compare matching five-minute intervals against vSphere performance charts using the same VM, datastore, read/write direction, rollup, and time zone. Retain chart export or screenshots, metric points, SPL job ID, add-on versions, dimension inventory, and arithmetic. Differences caused by chart rollup or delayed points must be understood before alerting. This review specifies the comparison but does not claim it has run.

Operate separate health checks for stale newest points, expected VMs/datastores with no series, missing dimensions, negative values, abrupt point-count changes, duplicate vCenter scope, unexpected host-scoped names, and metric disappearance after allowlist or upgrade changes. A healthy latency dashboard without proven coverage is not evidence that storage is healthy.

## Step 4 — Operationalize response, dashboards, and evidence

Build the table, trend, heat map, and source-health panels described in `visualization`. Default the focused trend to 24 hours, with seven-day baseline and 30-day capacity views. Restrict metric-index and inventory access according to infrastructure data policy; VM, vCenter, host, and datastore names can reveal architecture. Route a persistent critical-service finding to virtualization, storage, and application owners. Route lower-tier findings to performance/capacity review unless service objectives or corroborating failures require incident response.

The responder first verifies source freshness, metric names, immutable identity, datastore dimension, units, point counts, and two adjacent buckets. Next compare read versus write direction, peer VMs on the same datastore, the same VM's other datastores, hypervisor peers, IOPS and throughput, queue/device/kernel metrics if separately collected, vCenter tasks/events, backup/snapshot jobs, path state, array volume telemetry, and application latency/error objectives. Many peers on one datastore support a shared-storage hypothesis; one VM with high I/O can support workload-specific contention; neither pattern proves root cause. Capture the tested hypothesis and owner decision.

Retain the artifacts listed in `evidence` under the organization's operational policy. A screenshot without exact metric names, dimensions, search revision, two bucket values, and coverage state is insufficient. Keep `status=draft` until the target add-on version, vCenter scope, metric contract, positive/negative controls, vSphere comparison, threshold, source-health alert, notification, exception process, and runbook are validated and approved.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot product-specific failures

- **No VM datastore metrics:** verify Scheduler state, DCN registration, vCenter credentials/connectivity, collection assignment, VM scope, Metrics Indexes installation, and `vmware-perf-metrics` routing. ESXi syslog is not a replacement.
- **Read/write metrics absent while other VM metrics exist:** inspect VM metric allowlist/denylist values and vCenter counter availability. Use the exact conf parameter names from Splunk's metric reference; do not alias max latency or read/write rate to total latency.
- **Datastore is blank or aggregate:** verify VM instance-level collection and vCenter's available metric instances. Requalify cardinality after enabling it. Do not group an aggregate value under a guessed datastore.
- **VM identity is missing or changes:** use UUID/MOID as the throttle key and reconcile hierarchy/inventory collection. A display name is not an immutable identifier.
- **Values disagree with vSphere:** align entity, datastore instance, direction, interval, chart rollup, time zone, and unit. Remember this search averages vSphere average samples and is not request weighted.
- **Unexpected duplicate points:** inspect overlapping DCN/vCenter assignments, duplicate forwarding, dimension variants, and retries. Correct collection before raising persistence or thresholds.
- **Findings disappear after upgrade:** compare metric catalog, allow/deny configuration, source type, dimensions, index permissions, and compatible package versions before re-enabling the alert.
- **Point cadence is delayed:** measure `_time` freshness and scheduler/DCN health. Adjust the completion allowance only after proving normal delay; do not include partial buckets silently.
- **Only one direction has data:** confirm whether the workload performed reads or writes and whether the other metric exists in the catalog. The SPL can evaluate one direction, but missing coverage must remain visible in health panels.
- **High latency has no obvious array fault:** total latency includes kernel and device components and can reflect workload, queueing, fabric, path, array, or maintenance effects. Correlate the additional surfaces before assigning cause or changing storage.
grandmaExplanation: We watch how long each virtual machine waits when reading from or writing to each shared storage area. If that delay stays high across two checks, the right teams can compare the machine, storage, and current work before deciding what needs attention.
